subject: ventures/bike-shop-repair-profit-calculator
professional: an independent bicycle shop owner / service manager who prices repairs and tracks service-department margin; first checks: is the mechanic's paid-but-idle time in the labor cost (techs are paid by the clock hour, not the billed minute), does the job price cover shop overhead (a shop labor rate, not just direct cost), what is the effective rate per bench hour, and does a care plan's prepaid revenue get treated as presold rather than as more jobs

evidence.correctness: Ran the shipped plan() on sampleInput() (node scratchpad run.mjs) and recomputed by hand: loaded rate 22 x 1.12 = 24.64/h; flat 6.16 labor / 12.16 cost / 17.84 profit / 59.5%; tune 24.64 / 36.64 / 58.36; overhaul 73.92 / 118.92 / 141.08; care plan 5,960 - 40x3x12.16 = 4,500.80; contribution 51,619.20; fixed 750 + 21,000 + 4,000 = 25,750; profit 25,869.20; hours 845 of 1,564.2 (54%). All match, as do margin-on-price target prices (118.92 / 0.6 = 198.20) and care-plan break-even visits (149 / 12.16 = 12.25 -> 12.3). What is wrong is the model: technician pay is charged only for the bench minutes jobs use, so the 719.2 hours of the 1,564.2 'bench hours available' that sit idle cost nothing. With the tech paid for the scheduled bench hours (as an hourly mechanic is), the sample season makes 8,148.11, not 25,869.20, and the 50% volume row is -28,071.89, not +59.60. Break-even (589 jobs) scales the care-plan contribution with job count; treating the 4,500.80 of prepaid plans as presold gives 533. Arithmetic right, headline profit and break-even overstated: 2.
evidence.completeness: Every README-listed feature works end to end in calc.mjs and index.html: three services, burdened pay, profit per bench hour, target-margin price, tools amortised, rent for open months, care plan with break-even visits, utilization, break-even count, 50-150% table, share link (round-trips and drops unknown keys), CSV. Edge: a care-plan-only plan (all job counts 0, rent present) prints 'the services do not cover their own labor and materials ... Raise a price first' though every service has a positive margin, and with no fixed costs prints 'Break-even is about 0 paid jobs ... you plan 0'.
evidence.verification: node --test '*.test.mjs' from the subject dir: 28 tests, 28 pass. quality_mutate.py: 2 of 5 mutants caught (weeks 4.345 -> 4; break-even visits on price instead of cost). Survived: Math.ceil -> Math.floor on break-even jobs, the care-plan 'loses money past' comparison flipped, and the under-target-price flag loosened to 90% of target. The advice text that carries the decisions is barely asserted.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (155 lines), index.html, usage.mjs. Small, pure and readable, with input validation and a safe share link. Defects: blank fields silently become hidden defaults that differ from the page's own (blank tune-up price -> 55 and minutes -> 30 while the page shows 95 and 60; blank tech pay -> 22), calc.mjs:23-27; CSS rules for tr.drive / tr.dwell / tr.restart copied from another tool's template and unused; pass-only branch messaging wrong (calc.mjs:110-113).
evidence.claims: Disclaimer, no-warranty, privacy and a 'Not modelled' list are present (page.test.mjs asserts them); served-copy.mjs shows no retired origin left in llms.txt/sitemap/canonical after the deploy rewrite. Unbacked: 'Most shops jam on weekends: an average near 70% usually means peak weeks turn work away' (calc.mjs:122) has no source in the tree. The FAQ defines a care plan as 'free flat fixes and discounted tune-ups' but only flat-fix visits are modelled. The 'How much should a bike shop charge' FAQ presents direct cost / (1 - margin) as the price method, which leaves rent and tools unpriced. The not-modelled list omits the biggest assumption: unpaid idle technician time.
evidence.fitness: Walked the job: a service manager enters the season and gets a ranked per-bench-hour table and a profit number. The ranking (flat 96, tune 83, overhaul 71.67 per bench hour before pay) is usable and the care-plan visit break-even is a real help. But the decision the page sells (how many jobs cover the stands and rent, and the season at 50% volume) is overstated whenever the bench is not full, which is the normal case (54% in the example). Workaround (put the tech's scheduled pay in 'other fixed cost' and set pay to 0) is not stated.
evidence.domain: Compared with standard service-department costing (auto and bike shops alike: technicians on hourly pay are paid for clock hours, so labor cost per job = payroll / billed hours, and the posted shop labor rate is set to cover tech cost plus overhead at an expected productivity). The tool treats labor as a per-minute variable cost, has no productivity / efficiency input, and sets the target price on direct cost only, so a job 'at 40% margin' still carries none of the 25,750 of fixed cost. Burden 12% is low but labelled as an input. Departures are material, so 2.

defects.what: Technician pay is charged only for the bench minutes jobs use (labor = min/60 x loaded rate), so idle scheduled bench hours cost nothing. On the sample, 719.2 of 1,564.2 hours are idle; paying the mechanic for them (24.64/h) turns the 25,869.20 season profit into 8,148.11 and the 50% volume row from +59.60 into -28,071.89. Break-even and the volume table overstate whenever the bench is not full, and the not-modelled list does not say so.

Break-even job count multiplies fixed / total contribution by the job count, so the prepaid care-plan contribution is treated as if it grew with jobs: 589 on the sample where treating the 4,500.80 of plans as presold gives 533. With care plans only it prints 'the services do not cover their own labor and materials ... Raise a price first' though every service has a positive margin, and with no fixed cost 'Break-even is about 0 paid jobs ... you plan 0'.

Blank fields silently fall back to hidden defaults that differ from the page's own values: a cleared tune-up price becomes 55 (page shows 95), tune-up minutes 30 (page 60), tech pay 22, burden 12, margin 40, with no message.

The target-margin price is direct cost / (1 - margin) and the FAQ presents it as how a shop should price, but it carries none of the tools, rent and other fixed cost; there is no shop labor rate or productivity input, which is how service departments set prices.
Unbacked claim in the advice: 'Most shops jam on weekends: an average near 70% usually means peak weeks turn work away' has no source.
The FAQ defines the care plan as 'free flat fixes and discounted tune-ups' but only flat-fix visits are modelled.
Three of five seeded mutants survive (break-even rounding, the care-plan loses-money comparison, the under-target-price flag): the advice sentences that carry the decisions are barely asserted.
Unused CSS rules (tr.drive, tr.break, tr.dwell, tr.off, tr.restart) copied from another tool's template.

verdict: The arithmetic is right: per-service cost, margin, per-bench-hour figures, target prices, fixed cost, care-plan break-even visits and the season totals recompute exactly from the sample (profit 25,869.20). It misses the bar on what the headline means. The mechanic is paid only for the minutes jobs use, so idle bench hours are free; with the tech paid for the 1,564.2 scheduled hours the sample makes 8,148.11, and the 50% volume row is a 28,071.89 loss, not +59.60. Break-even counts prepaid care plans as if they scaled with jobs (589 vs 533), the target price ignores rent and tools, blank fields become hidden defaults (a cleared tune-up price is 55, not the 95 shown), and 3 of 5 seeded mutants survive. The per-bench-hour ranking and the care-plan visit check are genuinely useful; the profit, break-even and volume table would mislead a shop owner whose bench is not full.
